To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the X-ray pulse at synchrotrons can be used for time-resolved small-angle X-ray scattering experiments with a time resolution of about 1 picosecond and a spatial resolution of 10 nm.
we have shown that the time resolved pump-probe technique is capable of resolving the structural dynamics of laser excited gold nanoparticles on the nanometer-scale with high precision.

the pump-probe technique with X-ray pulses from synchrotron radiation sources is a powerful tool to study structural dynamics of nanoparticles in solution and that this technique is capable of being extended to the single-particle level with X-ray free-electrons lasers.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of X-ray scattering as a tool for the study of ultrafast dynamics in nanometer-scale objects.
the development of X-ray scattering techniques for the time-resolved study of photoinduced processes in nanoparticles.
the investigation of the structural dynamics of nanoparticles in the time domain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the experiments presented in this work demonstrate that the X-ray pulse train structure of synchrotron radiation is a unique and very useful probe for the study of structural dynamics in nanoparticles.
the experiments on femtoseconds laser-excited nanoparticles are a first step towards the study of single nanoparticles using X-ray free-electrons lasers.
the experiments presented are a proof of principle of time-resolved small-angle scattering experiments at synchrotrons and X-ray lasers.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the combination of X-ray scattering and ultrafast laser excitation provides the opportunity to study the structural dynamics of photoexcited matter with high temporal and spatial resolution.
we have shown that X-ray scattering experiments can be performed on the femtosecond timescale.

we have developed the technique to a state where we can study the structural changes in nanoparticles on the nanometer and femtosecond scale, and that the technique has been demonstrated to be applicable also to the X-ray free-electon laser.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the X-ray pump-probe experiments on single particles are within reach.
pump-probe experiments on the nanometer length scale with X-rays are feasible and will be a powerful tool for the study of nanometer-sized systems.
the X-ray free-electro laser is capable of resolving the structural dynamics of nanoparticles in the sub-picosecond regime.
